intro.heading: The photos exist. The question is where they go.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: Mrs Ellis moved in last Thursday. Her son, Tim, came for tea and said he had a shoebox of old prints at home: her wedding in 1962, the allotment, a week in Whitby with her sister Joan. He wants the staff to know who is who. The key worker says that would be wonderful and gives him the manager's mobile number. Tim sends six pictures that evening. They sit in a message thread on one phone, with no names on them, and the night team never sees any of them.

trail.text: Mrs Ellis moves in. Her son stays for tea.
Tim mentions a shoebox of family photos.
The key worker says, “Please send them. They will help.”
Six pictures arrive on the manager's own phone.
Nobody knows who Joan is, or where the allotment was.
A new carer cannot find a way into a conversation.
Tim asks if the photos helped. Nobody can say.
“How do you use what her family told you?” A phone is not an answer.

trail_close: The family did their part. The gap is between a kind offer and something the team can use safely. Here is how CareStream collects the photos, lets you check each one, and puts only the approved ones in front of staff.

why.heading: A dementia photo album is more than a nice idea
why.sub: Photos carry names, places and stories that a written profile can only hint at.

cards.title: A picture starts a conversation
cards.body: A carer who has never met Mrs Ellis can say, “Is that you in Whitby?” Life story photos give new and agency staff something warm to say, and the person something to answer.

cards.title: Care should reflect the person
cards.body: Care must reflect the person's preferences, and where someone cannot decide for themselves the Mental Capacity Act asks you to consider their past and present wishes and feelings, and to consult people who care about them. Family are often the best source.

cards.title: Photos need a careful gate
cards.body: A photo can show other people, or something the resident would not want shared. A manager should look at each one before the whole team does, and the files should not sit in a text thread.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: A relative wants to send photos for our dementia photo album. What do I do?
items.a: You invite them from the resident's record, with their name and email, and CareStream emails a private link. On that page they choose photos, add a caption and say who is in each one. Nothing reaches your team until you have looked at it.

items.q: Does the family need an account?
items.a: No. The link is the way in, with no login and no password. You can have up to 5 photos on one link, each up to 5MB, and once the family member presses send the link is spent. If they find more later, you send a new link.

items.q: What stops an unsuitable photo reaching staff?
items.a: You do. Every family photo waits on the Approvals tab. You can edit the caption and approve it, or reject it, and rejecting removes the file. Staff and the chat only ever see approved photos.
Yes. From the resident's record you can add a photo with a caption and a note on who is in it. Photos you add are approved at once, because you are the approver.
Signed in staff of your service, through short lived links. There is no public web address for a photo. Only approved photos of current residents are shown.

items.q: Does the chat look at what is in the picture?
items.a: No, and it says so if asked. It finds photos from the captions and notes people wrote, matched by meaning. So a good caption matters. A photo with no caption can still be shown when you look at that person's photos.

items.q: What happens if the resident passes away or moves on?
items.a: Their photos leave the hub straight away, and any photo still waiting is deleted. Approved files stay in private storage for the retention period, like the written profile, then are deleted with it.

items.q: Which plan is it on, and can I try it?
items.a: Resident profiles and photos are on Professional and above. There is a 14 day free trial, and the pricing page shows which plan includes it. You can create an account or book a demo to see it first.

limits.heading: Honest limits: a gathering tool, not a family account

cards.title: It is not a printed photo memory book
cards.body: CareStream shows approved photos to staff in the hub, with their captions. It does not lay them out as a keepsake you can print or give back to the family. If you want a photo memory book for a resident to enjoy, you would make that separately.

cards.title: Nothing is automatic
cards.body: Photos do not reach staff by themselves. A manager has to approve each one, so someone needs to check the Approvals tab. Photos that nobody approves stay hidden from the team.

cards.title: Captions do the work
cards.body: The chat cannot see inside a picture or describe it. A photo is found only by its caption and the note on who is in it, so a blank caption is hard to find. It is also on Professional and above, and the family cannot see the profile or message you.

faqs.heading: Family photos and resident profiles, answered

items.q: What is a dementia photo album in a care home?
items.a: It is a small, personal set of pictures of the person's family, places and past that staff and the person can look at together. In CareStream, approved photos sit with the resident's profile in the Staff Hub. Read more in our guide to the this is me document.

They are photos that tell part of someone's story: a wedding, a job, a pet, a holiday. Staff use them to start conversations and to understand who matters to the person. Captions that name people and places make them far more useful.

items.q: Is this a photo memory book?
items.a: Not quite. A photo memory book is usually a printed keepsake. CareStream keeps approved photos with captions for staff to use in the hub, and it does not print or lay them out.

items.q: Can the assistant describe what is in a photo?
items.a: No. It reads the captions and notes that people wrote, and shows the matching photos. It does not look inside a picture.

items.q: How many photos can a relative add, and what size?
items.a: Up to 5 photos on one link, each up to 5MB, as JPEG, PNG or WebP. Each is checked and saved again without location data.

items.q: Does a manager have to approve every photo?
items.a: Yes. A family photo stays hidden from staff until you approve it. You can edit the caption first, or reject it. Photos you add yourself from the resident record are approved at once.

items.q: Can the family see the photos we approve?
items.a: The family page only shows each photo they added, marked as waiting, approved or not used by the home. It does not show the profile or other photos.

items.q: What does the law say about including family?
items.a: Under section 4 of the Mental Capacity Act, people who care about someone should be consulted, where practicable, about what is in their best interests. Photos are one way family can show who the person is. Check your own policies on consent and sharing images.

guide.heading: How to build a good dementia photo album with families
guide.lede: A few habits make the difference between photos that sit unseen and ones that change how the team talks to someone. Ask early, ask for names, and check before you approve.

sections.h3: Ask for captions, not just pictures
paragraphs: The chat finds photos by their words. Tell relatives that a short caption such as “Wedding day, 1962” or “Whitby with Joan” is the most helpful thing they can add, and that the who is in it box helps staff learn the names.

Look at each photo as a new carer would, and as the resident might feel about it. Edit the caption so it is clear and kind. Reject anything that shows other people who might not want it shared, or anything the resident would find upsetting. You can read what the regulation expects in regulation 9 on person-centred care.
checklist: Is the person in the photo someone the resident would be glad to see?
Does the caption name the people and the place?
Does it show anyone else who might not want it shared?
Would a new carer know how to use it?

sections.h3: Close the loop with the team and the family
paragraphs: Tell the key worker when photos have been approved and show them how to ask the chat. Thank the relative personally. A dementia awareness course helps staff see why these details matter, and the Mental Capacity Act course covers wishes and best interests.

guide.note: This page describes how the software works and is not legal advice. Check your own policies and local guidance for how you collect and share images of residents.
